en: Preface to the *Biographies of the Great Master of Caoxi*:
When our progenitor, the Great Master who Transmitted the Teachings, sailed to the Tang to seek the Dharma, there were three traditions he transmitted:
the Tiantai Teaching, the Esoteric Vehicle, and the Chan Gate. At that time, in our own country, there existed only the Huayan and Vijñaptimātratā schools.
Although they have studied the teachings, they have never known the wondrous purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* or the profound meaning of the Esoteric Vehicle (*Guhyamantra-yāna*).
Consequently, they advocate exclusively for the Tiantai teachings and the Esoteric Vehicle, while regarding the Chan school as merely a lineage of transmission. As it has been said of old:

"The Tripitaka and twelve divisions of scripture are like painting a dragon; the principle of direct pointing is like dotting its eyes. Before the dragon is complete, where could one possibly apply those eyes?"
Jikaku and Chishō succeeded one another in entering China; they too devoted themselves exclusively to the Tiantai and Esoteric traditions.

After they had also studied the Chan school as a supplementary practice, the principles of the Perfect and Sudden and the doctrines of the Three Mysteries came to illuminate the four seas, and their teachings were fully established.
More than three hundred years later, the dragon was finally complete and its eyes could be opened. Then, figures such as Dōgen, Eshin, and Yōsai emerged from within our own school;
they were able to embody the intent of the successive patriarchs. They traveled to the Song and Yuan dynasties to receive the Dharma and transmit the mind, returning to Japan to proclaim it.
When the time arrived and the conditions were ripe, their influence swept across the realm. From this...

Observing this, one sees that the Zen of our own country originated with Saichō (Dengyō Daishi), branched out through Jikaku, Chishō, and Genshin, and spread to Yōsai and Dōgen, before finally converging into the various great patriarchs.
I am but a mere blade of grass within the gateway of the Teaching, one who recites the *Denpō-e* (Record of the Transmission of the Dharma) of Dengyō;
yet, I have privately cultivated myself in the direct pointing of the ultimate meaning, desiring to follow its form.
I have inherited this lineage. Thus, whenever scholars who frequent my gate possess a spark of Chan insight, I invariably urge them to investigate the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the school).
This is also because I look up to the lofty traces of Zuo Xi, who inspired Yongjia. An ancient said: "Chan is the mainstay of the Teaching; the Teaching is the net of Chan.
How could there be the mainstay of Chan without the net of the Teaching? And how could there be the net of the Teaching alone...

How could there be no guiding thread for Chan? Indeed, Chan possesses its teachings, yet its realization is profound and subtle. The pedagogical devices of Linji, for instance, were by no means superficial.
Teachings possess Chan, yet their application must be vital and spontaneous. The instructions of Siming, for example, were by no means mere contrived arrangements.
Therefore, those who practice Chan must master the teachings, and those who study the teachings must engage in Chan practice. Yet, in later generations...
Not realizing that the Three Studies share a single source, some have even gone so far as to divide the river and drink from separate streams—how lamentable this is!

The Zen practitioner Master Fang has brought forth the *Separate Transmission* (Biechuan) of the Great Master Caoxi, which was requested by Zhizhe (Zhendi). He requests that I compose a preface for it.
Beholding this noble undertaking, I shall write a preface concerning what our founder received in transmission and what he cherished within his breast. This is the transmission.
Regarding the points of agreement and divergence with the *Platform Sūtra* and other texts, these are fully detailed in Master Fang’s postscript; therefore, I shall not elaborate further here.
Written respectfully by the Koryŏ monk Kyŏng-ŭng in the summer of the twelfth year of the Baolì era, the Renwu year (1792).
The Separate Biography of the Great Master of Caoxi:
The Dharma-Transmission Principles of the Sixth Patriarch, National Teacher Huineng of Baolin Mountain at Caoxi in Shaozhou during the Tang Dynasty;
together with the Imperial Edict and bestowed items from Emperor Gaozong, the alteration of the temple’s name plaque, and the Great Master’s seal of approval.
The disciples, along with the six kinds of auspicious signs at his parinirvāṇa, and the prophetic records of Tripitaka Master Jñānaghoṣa, etc.
At the fifth day of the first month in the ninth year of the Renwu year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, there was a Brahmin Tripitaka Master named Jñānayaśas.
This was a Great Virtuous One (Bhadanta) from Nālandā Monastery in Central India. Taking leave of the king of that country, he came here to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.

At that time, several dozen disciples attended him as an entourage. He was a Tripitaka Master of vast learning and great erudition, well-versed in the study of the sūtras, śāstras, and the science of astrology.
With the resolve to propagate the Mahāyāna, he traveled through various countries, crossing the vast blue waves and sailing upon the ocean until he reached [this land].
At Caoxi Village in Shaoyou Prefecture, he said to the villagers, "Observe this water source;

there must be a superior site here suitable for the dwelling of śramaṇas, where eminent monks will appear in succession without end. I wish to seek it out. Upon arriving at Caoxi, he exhorted the villagers to construct a residence.
After five years had passed, he named the mountain gate the Baolin Monastery, which was revered by both humans and devas.

The entire realm turned to him for refuge. On the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifth year of the Tianjian era, an imperial decree was issued to the renowned monks and great virtuous ones throughout the empire, ordering them to enter the inner palace chapel (*nèidàochǎng*) to receive offerings.
At that time, Hou Gong, the Prefectural Governor of Shaozhou, presented the Tripitaka Master to the court. The Prefect asked the Tripitaka Master, "Why is this mountain gate named as it is?"
"Is it called Baolin (Jewel Grove)? He replied, "One hundred and seventy years after my departure, the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure shall flourish and transform beings in this place.
Because those who study there will be as numerous as a forest, it shall be named Baolin.

In the fourth month of that year, the Tripiṭaka Master obtained an imperial audience and was granted fifty *qǐng* of land by imperial decree for Baolin Monastery. In the tenth year of the Tiānjiān era, the Tripiṭaka Master entered the palace.
Shan returned to his native country. By the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, the world was in a state of chaos and ruin, and the monasteries were destroyed and abandoned.
In the first year of the Tianping era, Li Cangzhi, the Magistrate of Lechang County, requested the plaque of Baolin Monastery and established a temple in Lingxi Village of Lechang.
During the first year of the Xianheng era, Master Huineng—whose secular surname was Lu—was from Xinzhou.

He was a man who lost his parents at an early age and became an orphan at three years old. Although he lived among the common crowd, he possessed a resolute will for the life beyond the mundane world.
At that time, when the Great Master traveled to Caoxi, [Zhao] Jue formed a bond of righteousness with the villager Liu Zhilüe as brothers.
He was then thirty years of age. Zhilüe’s paternal aunt had left the household life and was ordained at Shanjian Temple under the name Wujin.
Zang constantly recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. During the day, the Great Master would provide manual labor for her; at night, he would listen to the sutra.
By dawn, he had explained its meaning to the nun Wujinzang. When the nun brought the sutra to him to read, the Great Master said, "I do not recognize written characters."

The nun said, "Since you do not recognize characters, how can you explain their meaning? The Master replied, "The principle of Buddha-nature is not something that can be understood through words and letters.
That you do not recognize them now—why should it be strange? When the people heard this, they all sighed in admiration, saying: [They were moved by his words.]
His insight was such that his celestial faculties were spontaneously awakened; it was beyond the reach of ordinary men. He was fit to leave the household life and dwell in this Bao Lin Temple.
The Great Master then resided in this temple and practiced the Way for three years.

This was precisely the time foretold by Tripiṭaka Master Jñānayaśas one hundred and seventy years prior. At that time, the Master was thirty-three years of age. Later, he heard [the news] from Lechang.
At the stone cave west of the county, there was Master Yuan; he subsequently went there to study seated meditation (*zuo chan*).

The Great Master had never previously studied calligraphy, nor had he ever perused the sutras or śāstras. At that time, there was Meditation Master Huiji, who was reciting the *Tou-tuo jing* (Sūtra on the Dhuta Practices).

Upon hearing the sūtra, the Great Master sighed and said, "The meaning of the sūtra is such as this; what is the use of my sitting here in vain? This occurred in the fifth year of the Xianheng era. The Great Master...
At the age of thirty-four, Master Huìjì Cànshī said to the Great Master, "I have long heard that Master Rèn of Mount Huángméi in Qí Prefecture has opened the gate of Chan;
you should go there to study. On the third day of the first month of that year, the Great Master set out from Shāozhōu for Dōngshān to seek Master Rèn.
Carrying his staff and walking barefoot, he traveled alone until he reached Hóngzhōu.

On the eastern road, there were frequently many fierce tigers. The Great Master traveled alone through the mountains and forests without fear. He eventually reached Mount Dong and met the Great Master Ren.
The Great Master Ren asked, "Have you come to transform sentient beings? Nan replied, "I have come solely seeking to become a Buddha.
The Great Master Ren asked, "Where are you from? Nan replied, "I am a man from Xinzhou in Lingnan. The Great Master Ren said, "You are from Ling..."

A man from Xinzhou in Nanhai. When asked, "Can you become a Buddha? he was able to reply, "What difference is there between the Buddha-nature of a man from Xinzhou in Lingnan and the Buddha-nature of the Upādhyāya?
Master Ren did not ask him further; it may be said that he recognized his own Buddha-nature.
He attained sudden enlightenment into True Suchness (Tathatā). How profound and marvelous! Master Ren had a great many disciples in the mountains;

looking around at his left and right, he saw they were all like dragons and elephants. He then ordered Neng to enter the kitchen to provide offerings. For eight months, Neng was able to endure hardships without flinching.
Suddenly, while others were joking and playing together, Neng remained solemn and unconcerned, forgetting his own person for the sake of the Way, and continued to tread [his duties].
Dun-neng was pounding rice at a millstone. Feeling that his body was too light, he tied a large stone to his waist to increase the weight of the pestle; consequently, he injured his waist and legs.
When Master Zhiyi arrived at the site where Dun-neng was milling rice, he asked, "For the sake of making offerings, you have injured your waist and legs.
How is the pain? Dun-neng replied, "I do not perceive a body; who would speak of pain? That night, Master Zhiyi summoned Dun-neng to enter [the samādhi].
In the quarters, the Master asked, "When you first arrived, you told me you were a person from Lingnan.
What difference is there between your Buddha-nature and that of the Upādhyāya? Who taught you this? He replied, "Buddha-nature is not partial; there is no distinction between the Upādhyāya and me."
This applies equally to all sentient beings; there is no further distinction between them, though it merely follows the faculties [of individuals] as to whether it is hidden or manifest.
Master Zhi Ren questioned him, saying, "Buddha-nature is formless; how can it be hidden or manifest? Daoren was able to answer, "Buddha-nature is formless;
when awakened to, it is manifest; when deluded, it is hidden. At that time, the disciples of Master Zhi Ren saw that Daoren was debating the meaning of Buddha-nature with his Upādhyāya.
The Great Master, knowing that his followers did not understand, sent the multitude away for the time being. Then the Great Master Kṣānti said to Neng:
"When the Tathāgata was approaching parinirvāṇa, he entrusted the Dharma of the profound Prajñāpāramitā to Mahākāśyapa."
Kāśyapa entrusted it to Ānanda; Ānanda entrusted it to Śaṇavāsa; Śaṇavāsa entrusted it to Upagupta.
Thereafter, it was transmitted in succession through the Western Regions, passing through twenty-eight patriarchs until it reached the Great Master Dharmatrāta.
"In the land of Han, I am the First Patriarch. I have entrusted [the Dharma] to Huike; Huike entrusted it to Daoxian; Daoxian entrusted it to Shuangfeng Xin;

and Xin has entrusted it to me. I now wish to depart. The Dharma is entrusted to you; you must guard and protect it so that it does not come to an end. Nan said: [The text continues: "I am able [to do so]."
Nanren is capable, yet he is not fit to receive the transmission of the Buddha-nature. Here in this place, there are many dragons and elephants. Master Ren said:
"Although there are many dragons and elephants here, I know their depths and shallows; they are like rabbits and horses, whereas only the elephant king is worthy of my entrustment."
National Teacher Ren was about to entrust the robe he had received to National Teacher Neng. The Master [Neng] then bowed his head in reverence and accepted it.
The Master asked the Upādhyāya, "The Dharma is without words; it is transmitted from mind to mind and from Dharma to Dharma. What is the purpose of this robe?
National Teacher Ren replied, "The robe is the token of faith for the Dharma, and the Dharma is the principle of the robe. This has been transmitted from the ancestors; there is nothing else."
Appendix. If it is not the robe, the Dharma is not transmitted; if it is not the Dharma, the robe is not transmitted.
The robe is that which was handed down by the Venerable Siṃha of the Western Land to ensure that the Buddha-Dharma would not be interrupted. The Dharma is the Tathāgata’s profound Prajñā.
To know that Prajñā is empty, quiescent, and non-abiding is to realize the Dharmakāya. To see that the Buddha-nature is empty, quiescent, and non-abiding is true liberation.
"You may take this robe and depart. He then accepted it and did not dare disobey the command. However, this Dharma-transmitting kāṣāya was made of Central Indian cloth;
in Sanskrit it is called *pārāna*, which in the language of Tang means "the finest cloth. It is made from the cotton flower (*tūla*).
At the time of its production, people did not recognize it and erroneously called it "silk cloth. Master Jin (Renzong) said to Huineng: "You must go quickly; I shall see you off."
Upon arriving at Jiuzhang Station in Qizhou, Master Ren told Huineng: "You, who transmit the Dharma, will encounter many obstacles in the future.

Huineng asked the Master, "Why will there be so many difficulties? Ren replied, "In the future, there will be heterodox teachings that will compete for influence, attaching themselves to kings and high ministers to obscure my True Dharma.
You should go on your way with care. Huineng then paid his respects and took his leave, traveling southward. Master Ren—
After the Great Master had seen them off, he returned to Dongshan. He remained silent, without further words. The disciples were startled and asked, "Why does the Upādhyāya not speak?
The Great Master addressed the assembly, saying, "When the multitude has dispersed, there will be no Buddha-dharma here.
The Buddha-dharma has already gone south. I shall not speak now; you will know it for yourselves later. The Great Master Ren was uniquely capable of great things.
The Master remained for three days, after which he again addressed his disciples, saying, "The Great Dharma has been propagated; I shall now pass away.
When the Great Master Ren passed into *nirvāṇa*, all manner of birds cried out in mourning, a wondrous fragrance filled the air, the sun lost its brilliance, and wind and rain broke the trees.
At that time, there was a man of the fourth rank of officialdom, a layman surnamed Chen, who renounced worldly life to become a monk under the Upādhyāya, receiving the name Chan Master Huiming.
Hearing that Master Huineng was departing with the robe and bowl, Huiming rushed after him toward the south. Eventually, he caught up with Master Huineng at Dayu Ridge.
Master Huineng immediately returned the robe and bowl to Huiming. Huiming said, "I did not come for the sake of the robe and bowl.
I wonder, Master, what further words of instruction were given when you first received the entrustment? I pray you will grant me your guidance. Master Huineng then spoke for him.
Master Ming transmitted the secret instructions to him. Huiming accepted the teaching with reverence and immediately took his leave.
Master Ming said to Huineng, "Go quickly! Go quickly! There will be many people coming after you. Master Neng then traveled south.
The following morning, as expected, several hundred people arrived; they reached the mountain pass and saw Master Ming. The Master said, "I have already—"
Having arrived here, he did not see this man; he asked those coming from the south, but they too did not see him. Suffering from a foot ailment, he calculated that [the time] had not yet passed.
These people then turned back and searched toward the north. Master Ming, having received the oral instructions, was still not enlightened;

he remained at the Peak Temple on Mount Lu for three years before finally realizing the esoteric words. Later, Master Ming resided at Mount Meng, where he extensively transformed all classes of beings. He was able to...
The Great Master returned to the South and traveled briefly to Caoqi.
Still being pursued by those seeking him, he took refuge in the border between the two counties of Sihui and Huaiji in Guangzhou. He remained there for five years among hunters.
At the age of thirty-nine, in the first year of the Yifeng era, he first attended the lectures on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* given by Dharma Master Yinzong at Zhizhi Temple in Guangzhou.
The *Pan jing*. The Dharma Master was a native of Jiangdong. The Zhiyi Temple where he resided was established by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty;
it is the present-day Longxing Temple in Guangzhou. The Dharma Master frequently exhorted his disciples to engage in formal debate on doctrinal points.
On one occasion, he instructed them to hoist a banner on the thirteenth day of the first month. That night, as the assembly discussed the meaning of the banner, the Dharma Master was in the corridor.

Listening from the next room, he heard that the first debater claimed: "The banner is insentient; it moves because of the wind. The second person challenged him, saying: "Both the wind and the banner are insentient;
how can there be movement? The third person said: "Because causes and conditions harmonize, they move together.
The fourth person stated: "The banner does not move; it is the wind that moves of its own accord. The crowd’s contentious debate continued in a clamorous uproar without ceasing.
The Great Master Neng called out loudly to stop the people, saying, "The banner does not move in any other way; that which you call 'moving' is simply the mind of the person moving of its own accord.
Upon hearing this, Dharma Master Yinzong waited until the lecture was nearly finished the following day and asked the assembly, "Last night, there was a debate in a certain room;
who was the one who spoke last? This person must have received instruction from an excellent teacher."
The artisan. Among them was a fellow resident who said, "This is the Lay Practitioner Lu from Xinzhou. The Dharma Master said, "I invite the practitioner to come to my room.
He was able to go to the room as requested. The Dharma Master asked, "Whom have you served? Nanquan replied, "I served the Great Master Ren of Dongshan in Qizhou, north of the Ling Mountains.
The Dharma Master asked again, "What did the Great Master Ren say regarding the Buddha-dharma at the time of his death?"
He turned toward the south and asked, "Are you not perhaps the Venerable One? [Huineng] replied, "I am. Since he said he was, [the Master] requested to see the robe transmitted for the Dharma.
Once Yinzong had seen the robe, he paid it profound respect with prostrations; his heart was filled with great joy, and he sighed in praise, saying:
"How unexpected it is that there is such an unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma in the South!

The Master of the Law asked, "How did the Great Master Ren entrust [the teaching], and what were his instructions and verbal teachings? The Great Master Neng replied, "He spoke only of seeing one's nature;

he did not speak of dhyāna-concentration, liberation, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), or the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). The Master of the Law asked, "Why did he not speak of dhyāna-concentration, liberation, the outflow-free, or the unconditioned?"
Neng replied, "Because these many dharmas are not the Buddha-nature. The Buddha-nature is the dharma of non-duality.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that this Buddha-nature is the dharma of non-duality; this is precisely Chan. The Dharma Master asked again, "In what way is the Buddha-nature the dharma of non-duality?
Neng said, "In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Gao-gui-de-wang addressed the Buddha, saying:"
“World-Honored One, regarding those who have committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or who are icchantikas—do they sever their roots of goodness?
Is their Buddha-nature altered? The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Noble Virtue King: “There are two kinds of roots of goodness:
first, the permanent; second, the impermanent. The Buddha-nature is neither permanent nor impermanent; therefore, it is not severed. This is called ‘non-duality. First,”
"Good. Second, there is the unwholesome. Buddha-nature is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; therefore it is uninterrupted and is called non-dual. Furthermore, it is said:
'Ordinary people perceive the aggregates (skandhas) and the elements (dhātus) as two, but the wise understand that their nature is non-dual.
This non-dual nature is the true nature. Ordinary people perceive clarity and ignorance as two, but the wise understand their nature."
There is no duality. The nature of non-duality is precisely the true nature (*tathatā*). The true nature is non-dual. Master Daishi said to the Dharma Master:
"Therefore, one knows that Buddha-nature is the Dharma of non-duality. Upon hearing this explanation, Yinzong immediately rose, joined his palms, and paid homage.
With sincere devotion, he took him as his teacher. The following day, during the lecture, he addressed the assembly, saying: "How fortunate is Yinzong!

Though I am but an ordinary person, I did not expect that a Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body would sit beneath me. What Yinzong has preached to the assembly regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is like mere rubble;
last night, when I invited the Venerable Lu to my quarters to discuss the meaning of the teachings, it was like gold and jade. Thus spoke to all the people.
Whether you believe it or not, this worthy one is the person to whom the Great Master Ren of Dongshan transmitted the Dharma.

Although no one has ever believed this, I request that the practitioner present the Dharma-transmission robe to everyone. Once they have seen it, they will prostrate and all will give rise to faith and reverence.
On the seventeenth day of the first month of the first year of the Yifeng era, Yinzong and the Great Master Neng shaved their heads.
He arrived at Luofu. On the eighth day of the second month, he received the precepts at Faxing Temple. The ordination platform was established by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of the Song Dynasty.
At that time, he had recorded in a prophecy: "In the future, an Arhat shall ascend this platform, and a Bodhisattva shall receive the precepts here.
The present Great Master Neng’s reception of the precepts fulfilled this prediction (*from the Biographies of Eminent Monks*). The Great Master Neng.
The Preceptor for Receiving the Precepts was Master Zhiguang of Zongchi Monastery in the Western Capital;
the Karmācārya was Master Huìjìng of Língguāng Monastery in Sūzhōu; and the Ācārya for Instruction was Master Dàoyìng of Tiānhuáng Monastery in Jīngzhōu.
Later, all three masters studied the Way under Great Master Nénghuì and passed away at Cáoqī. These were the virtuous ones who certified the precepts.
The first was the Vinaya Master Jñānagupta from Central India; the second was the Tripitaka Master Mitrasena.

These two Venerable Ones were both Arhats, profoundly learned in the Tripiṭaka, and skilled in the dialects of Madhyadeśa and Aparāntaka. Dharma Master Yin Zong invited them to serve as his honored witnesses.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty under the Xiao clan, there was the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. He planted two *bodhi* trees beside the altar and addressed the assembly of monks, saying:
"Take good care of these trees; in the future, bodhisattva-monks will expound the Unsurpassed Vehicle beneath them."
Later, the Great Master sat beneath this tree and opened the Dharma-gate of the Eastern Mountain for the multitude.

This is recorded by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha (from the *Biography of the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha*). On the eighth day of the fourth month of that year, the Great Master first opened the Dharma-gate for the great assembly, saying:
"I have a Dharma that has no name and no character; it has no eyes, no ears, no body, and no mind."
It is called "Non-indication. It has no beginning and no end; it is neither internal nor external, nor is there a middle.
It neither departs nor arrives. It is not blue, yellow, red, white, or black; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is neither cause nor effect.
The Great Master asked the assembly, "What is this? The multitude looked at one another in pairs, not daring to answer. At that time, there was a young novice monk from Heze Temple named Shen.
Huì was thirteen years old at the time. He replied, "This is the fundamental source of the Buddhas. The Master asked, "What is this fundamental source?
The śrāmaṇera replied, "The fundamental source is the original nature of all Buddhas. The Master said, "I speak of that which has no name and no character."
"How can you say that Buddha-nature has a name? The śrāmaṇera replied, "Buddha-nature has no name;
it is because of my preceptor’s question that a name is established. At the very moment the name is established, there is no name. The Master struck the śrāmaṇera several times.
The assembly bowed in thanks and said, "This śrāmaṇera is but a small person who has troubled the Upādhyāya. The Great Master said, "Let the assembly disperse for now;
leave this talkative śrāmaṇera behind. When night fell, the Great Master asked the śrāmaṇera, "When I struck you, did your Buddha-nature feel it?
He replied, "Buddha-nature does not feel. The Great Master asked, "Did you know the pain? The śrāmaṇera replied, "I knew it."
[The Master] asked, "Since you know pain, why do you say that the Buddha-nature has no sensation? The śrāmaṇera replied, "How could it be the same as wood or stone?

Though there is pain, the nature of the mind does not experience it. The Master said to the śrāmaṇera, "When one's limbs are severed joint by joint and no anger or resentment arises, this is called 'no sensation.
I have forgotten my own body for the sake of the Way; I have been treading the pestle until my thighs were worn through."
He regarded them as suffering and named this state "Non-reception" (*asaṃvedana*). When you were struck now, your mental nature did not receive it.

You received all tactile sensations as if realizing the true and correct Samādhi of Reception. The śrāmaṇera secretly received his instructions. The Great Master left home to propagate the Dharma and receive the precepts;
when he reached the age of forty, Dharma Master Yin Zong invited the Great Master to return to Zhiyi Temple. Now, at Long... Guangzhou.
The Sutra Repository Hall of Xing Temple was where the Great Master established his Dharma hall. The Dharma Master asked the Great Master, "Where have you been residing for so long?
The Great Master replied, "Fifty *li* south of Qu County in Shaozhou, at the old Baolin Temple in Caoxi Village.
When the Dharma Master finished lecturing on the sutra, he escorted more than three thousand monastics and laypeople to see the Great Master back to Caoxi. Because of this—

He extensively propagated the Chan school, with disciples numbering one hundred thousand. On the fifteenth day of the first month of the first year of the Shénlóng era, an imperial edict invited the Great Master to enter the palace;
he submitted a memorial declining and would not go. Emperor Gāozōng Dàdì issued an edict stating:

"I venerate the Way with sincere devotion and thirst for the Chan school. I have summoned the Chan masters from the famous mountains of various provinces to assemble at the Inner Dao-chamber for offerings."
The two masters Dao’an and Hui-xiu are the foremost among the monastic community. I have frequently sought their counsel.

Furthermore, I have heard that in the south there is the Venerable Neng, who secretly received the prophetic transmission from Master Zhi-ru. He inherited the robe and bowl of Bodhidharma as a token of the Dharma, attained sudden enlightenment in the Supreme Vehicle, and clearly perceives the Buddha-nature.
He now resides at Mount Caoxi in Shaozhou, instructing and awakening sentient beings that "the mind itself is the Buddha."

"I have heard that the Tathāgata transmitted the mind through the mind and entrusted it to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa passed it down in succession until it reached Bodhidharma, whose teachings spread to this eastern land.

Transmitted from generation to generation, they continue unbroken to this day. Since you, Master, have received this inheritance and have a foundation upon which to rely, you may go to the capital to propagate the transformation [of sentient beings].
Monastics and laypeople alike will take refuge in you, and devas and humans will look up to you in reverence. Therefore, I have dispatched the Palace Attendant Xue..."
A Brief Invitation to the Master: We pray that you will descend to us at your earliest convenience. Issued on the fifteenth day of the first month of the first year of the Shenglong era.
Submitted by Śākyamuni Huineng of Caoxi Mountain in Shaoyou Prefecture, declining [the summons] due to illness.
Huineng was born in a remote region; from childhood, he aspired to the Way. By great fortune, he was entrusted with the Tathāgata’s mind by the Great Master Bodhidharma.

Seal. Transmitting the robe and bowl to the Western lands, he bestowed the Buddha-mind upon this Eastern soil. By imperial decree, the Palace Envoy Xue Jian was dispatched to summon Huineng to the inner court.
Huineng has long resided among the mountains and forests; now advanced in years, he suffers from wind-related ailments.

Your Majesty’s virtue encompasses all beyond the mundane world, and your Way penetrates the myriad people. You nurture the common folk and show benevolence to the masses, propagating the Great Teaching and revering the Śākya.

Seal. I, Shi Jiahui Neng, humbly submit this memorial while residing in the mountains to cultivate my practice and sustain my illness, so as to repay the Imperial Grace above and extend its benefits to the various princes and crown princes below.
I, Shi Jiahui Neng, prostrate myself again and again.
The imperial messenger Xue Jian asked the Great Master, "The virtuous Chan masters of the capital teach people that they must rely on sitting meditation (*zuo chan*).

They say that without the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is impossible to attain liberation and realize the Way. The Great Master replied, "The Way is realized through the awakening of the mind;
how could it depend on sitting? As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: 'If anyone says that the Tathāgata sits or lies down, that person does not understand my meaning.'"
Regarding the meaning that has been explained: the Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
To come from nowhere is called "birth," and to go nowhere is called "extinction. If there is neither birth nor extinction, this is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.
That all phenomena are empty is itself "sitting. The Great Master addressed the messenger, saying: "The Way is ultimately without attainment and without realization."
"How much more so for sitting meditation? Xue Jian said, "When I arrive at the Imperial Court, the Sage will surely question me.

I humbly pray that you, Master, will instruct me in the essentials of the mind, so that I may transmit them to the Sage and to those who study the Way in the capital. Like a lamp passed on to illuminate others, let those in darkness all become enlightened;
let this clarity be inexhaustible. The Great Master said, "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the principle of succession."
Luminosity is both inexhaustible and exhaustible; these names are established in mutual dependence. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Dharmas have no peer, for they are not established through mutual dependence. Xue Jian said: "Luminosity is a metaphor for wisdom, and darkness is a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).
If a practitioner of the Way does not employ wisdom to illuminate birth-and-death and afflictions, how can they attain liberation? The Great Master said: "Afflictions are themselves Bodhi."
"Ti. There is neither duality nor distinction. That you perceive wisdom as being able to illuminate is the view of the Two Vehicles.
A person of true wisdom does not see it in this way. Xuejian asked, "Great Master, what is the view of the Mahayana?
The Great Master replied, "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: 'Ordinary people perceive brightness and ignorance as two; the wise thoroughly understand their nature.'"
There is no duality. The nature of non-duality is the true nature. The true nature is the Buddha-nature.
The Buddha-nature does not decrease in ordinary beings, nor does it increase in sages and saints. It is not defiled by afflictions, nor is it purified by meditative concentration.
Neither discontinuous nor eternal; neither coming nor going; nor existing in between, nor within or without; neither arising nor ceasing;

its nature and characteristics are eternally abiding, forever unchanging and immutable. Xue Jian asked: "The Great Master speaks of non-arising and non-ceasing; how does this differ from the non-Buddhists?
The non-Buddhists also speak of non-arising and non-ceasing. The Great Master replied: "When the non-Buddhists speak of non-arising and non-ceasing..."

"Regarding that which is about to arise, it is already stilled and extinguished; though it is extinguished, it is not yet extinguished. I say that it is originally unborn, and thus now it is unextinguished.
This is not like the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), for whom there is nothing extraordinary; this is what makes us different. The Great Master said to Xue Jian:

'If you wish to grasp the essential point of the mind, do not engage in any deliberation regarding good or evil. The substance of the mind is profoundly still and tranquil, while its functioning is sovereign and free.'"
Xue Jian attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words and said, "Great Master, today I have finally realized that Buddha-nature is inherently present from the beginning.
Previously, I took it to be something far away; today I have finally realized that the Ultimate Way is not remote—it is right here as one practices.
Today I have finally realized that Nirvana is not distant—enlightenment (bodhi) is encountered at every turn. Today I have finally realized that Buddha-nature does not dwell on good or evil."

There is no thought, no recollection, no cognition, and no action; there is no abiding. Only today do I know that the Buddha-nature is eternally present and unchanging, and cannot be shifted by any evils.
The Imperial Messenger Xue Jian took his leave of the Great Master and departed for the capital with the memorial.
The Great Emperor Gaozong bestowed upon him a set of *morna* (worn-out) *kāṣāya* and five hundred rolls of silk. The imperial edict stated: "An edict to the Master:

Though you are aged and infirm, you cultivate the Way for our sake; you are the field of merit for the nation. If the Master, like Vimalakīrti, feigns illness, you shall propagate the Great Dharma as the Golden Grain [Bodhisattva] did.
Transmitting the mind of all Buddhas, you discourse on the teaching of non-duality, closing your mouth in silence at Vaiśālī."
Upon hearing the reprimand, the Bodhisattva withdrew. "If the Master is like this," [he thought]. Xue Jian transmitted the Master’s instructions on the wisdom and vision of the Tathāgata:
"Do not deliberate at all upon good or evil; you will naturally enter the essence of mind, which is limpid and eternally quiescent, its wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

"By the accumulated blessings of my past merits and the seeds of wholesome causes planted in former lives, I have encountered the appearance of the Master in this world and received the Master’s grace."
The Sudden Vehicle is the foremost of the Buddha-mind. I, the Emperor, am deeply moved by the Master’s grace; I shall wear it upon my head and practice it throughout eternity, never to decay.
I respectfully present one robe of *mònà* (linen) and five hundred rolls of silk as an offering to the Great Master.

Issued on the second day of the fourth month in the third year of the Shénlóng era. Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued on the eighteenth day of the eleventh month in the third year of the Shénlóng era. [Issued from] Sháo.
The common people of the province may repair the Buddha hall and the scripture repository of the Great Master’s Zhongxing Temple;
it shall be granted the name Fajian Temple. Since the Great Master’s place of birth was Xinzhou, his former residence shall be made Guoen Temple.

In the first year of the Yanhe era, the Great Master returned to Xinzhou to repair Guoen Temple. His disciples asked: "Venerable Sir, you are going to repair the temple; will you pass away there or not?"
"Returning! Who else is there capable of being consulted? The Master said, "The monk Lingzhen of Wengshan Temple, though afflicted by a lame foot, is not lame in heart.
My disciple should request him to preach the Dharma. He asked again, "When will the Master be able to return?"
He replied, "The day of my departure has arrived. While the Great Master was still alive, in the second year of the Jingyun era, he first constructed a niche and stupa at Caoxi.
Later, in the seventh month of the second year of the Tianjian era, the corridors and halls were not yet finished; he urged that they be completed early, saying, 'I shall depart.
My disciples did not yet understand his intent. In the eighth month of a certain year, the Great Master fell ill. All the disciples—"
He asked the Master, "To whom should the Dharma be entrusted? The Master replied, "The Dharma is not to be entrusted; furthermore, there is no one who can receive it.

Shenhui asked the Master, "Why is the robe of the transmission of the Dharma not transmitted? The Master replied, "If this robe were transmitted, those who transmit the Dharma would have short lifespans.
By not transmitting this robe, my Dharma will flourish and spread. It shall remain as a guardian at Caoxi. After my parinirvāṇa, seventy..."

After several years, there were two Bodhisattvas coming from the East: one was a lay Bodhisattva who constructed monasteries and dwellings, and the other was an ordained Bodhisattva who rebuilt the gates of our teaching.
A disciple asked the Great Master, "Why is it that this robe is transmitted to those of short lifespan? He replied:
"I have worn these robes three times. An assassin has come to take my life; my life hangs by a thread.

Fearing that those who shall transmit the Dharma hereafter may be harmed, I do not bestow them upon you. With great effort despite his illness, the Great Master exhorted his disciples to seek the Way while forgetting their own bodies, urging them to apply themselves with diligence to practice and proceed directly toward Bodhi.
On the third day of such-and-such month, he suddenly passed away while sitting upright.
He passed away at the age of seventy-six. On the day of his *parinirvāṇa*, smoke and clouds rose up suddenly; springs and ponds dried up; streams in the gullies and ravines ceased to flow;
and a white rainbow pierced the sun. To the east of the cliff, several thousand birds suddenly began to wail mournfully from the trees.
Furthermore, to the west of the temple, a white vapor like a length of silk, over a li long, rose straight upward alone against a clear and bright sky. It continued for—
The assembly dispersed after five days. Furthermore, five-colored clouds were seen in the southwest;
on that day, while there were no clouds in the four directions, several gusts of cool wind suddenly blew into the temple buildings from the southwest.
In an instant, a fragrant aroma filled the corridors and halls, the earth shook everywhere, and mountain cliffs collapsed. The Great Master passed away at Guangguo Temple in Xinzhou. The temple—
A threefold rainbow light appeared over the western mountain for ten days. Furthermore, at Chengtou Village in front of the monastery, a rainbow light appeared for one hundred days.
Various birds cried out in lamentation, and the spring water became like thick gruel, failing to flow for several days.
Moreover, at Wengshan Monastery, while Chan Master Zhen was preaching the Dharma to the assembly in front of his quarters during the night, a single beam of rainbow light emerged from the south.
He entered the quarters. The Zen Master addressed the assembly, saying, "The Upādhyāya has likely passed away in Xin Prefecture;
this rainbow light is a spiritual omen of the Upādhyāya. Shortly thereafter, a letter arrived from Xin Prefecture reporting the death, and the disciples of Caoxi broke into mourning.

Because the rainbow light suddenly vanished, the spring water gradually began to flow. When the letter reached Master Zhen of Wengshan, who heard the news of the lamentation, he established a thirty-seven-day *zhāi* (fasting) ceremony at night.
As monks and laypeople gathered in full, a rainbow light suddenly emerged from the master’s quarters.
Master Zhen told the assembly, "I shall not remain much longer. As the Sūtra says: "When the great elephant has departed, the young elephants follow as well. That very evening...
He passed away lying on his right side at midnight. The disciples of Caoxi escorted the Master’s entire body back to Caoxi;
however, the local officials at that time refused to release it, wishing instead to enshrine it in Guoen Temple to erect a stupa and offer worship.

Only after the disciples, including the monk Chongyi and others, presented their arguments to the Prefectural Governor was the body returned to Caoxi. Prior to this, the Master’s head and neck had already been encased in iron plates.
The body was wrapped and sealed with lacquer and glue. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, his spirit was moved into the sarcophagus.
In the twenty-seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, an assassin came to take his head; as the head moved out into the courtyard, the master struck it several times with a blade.
The crowd heard only the sound of metal, and upon waking from their alarm, they saw a filial son fleeing from the temple. They followed his tracks...
[The request] was not granted. When the Great Master was alive, he received the precepts, opened the Dharma for others, and guided disciples for thirty-six years.

He entered *nirvāṇa* in the second year of the Xiāntián era, the *rénzǐ* year (712 CE). Calculating from that year until the second year of the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty (781 CE), it amounts to seventy-one years.
In that year, the assembly requested his senior disciple, Xíngtáo, to maintain the robe transmitted [to him]. After thirty-five years had passed, there was a Palace Attendant...
The Censor Wei Ju erected a stele for the Great Master.

Later, the lay disciple of the Northern School, Wu Pingyi, in the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, rubbed away the inscription of Wei Ju’s stele and composed his own inscription bearing the name "Wu Pingyi.

In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era, there was Chan Master Huang of Tanzhou, who had previously served the Great Master Ren; he later returned to Lushan Temple in Changsha, where he constantly practiced.

While practicing seated meditation, he would occasionally enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and perceive sounds from both near and far. At that time, the Chan Master Daorong was residing at Caoxi, serving the Great Master for thirty years.
The Great Master often said to Rong, "You have successfully transformed sentient beings.

Rong then paid his respects and took leave to return north. On his way, he passed by the abode of Chan Master Huang. Rong prostrated himself and asked Huang, "I have heard that you, O Venerable One, always..."
"Upon entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), is there a mind present, or is there no mind?

If there is a mind, then all sentient beings possess minds and should likewise be able to enter meditative concentration. If there is no mind, then grass, trees, tiles, and pebbles should also be able to enter meditative concentration.
Wang replied, "When I enter meditative concentration, I have no such mind of 'existence' or 'non-existence. Rong replied, "If you have no mind of existence or non-existence, then..."
"This is constant concentration. Constant concentration has no entering or exiting; it is simply non-confrontation. Huáng asked, "You have come from the Great Master Néngruì;
with what Dharma did the Great Master instruct you? Yóngxīng replied, "The Great Master instructed me that there is neither fixedness nor confusion."
"Not sitting, not practicing dhyāna—this is the Tathāgata’s dhyāna. At these words, Huáng attained awakening;

he realized that the five aggregates do not exist and the six sense-objects are empty in essence. It is neither quiescence nor illumination; it is free from existence and free from emptiness, dwelling in neither the middle nor the extremes.

It is without effort and without merit, yet its application is sovereign and its Buddha-nature is perfectly penetrating. He sighed and said, "For thirty years, I have been sitting in vain. He then went to Cáo.

Xī took refuge with the Great Master and studied the Way. According to worldly tradition, Chan Master Huáng had been practicing seated meditation for thirty years before he recently resolved his mind to cultivate the Way.
In the second year of the Jingyún era, he returned to his former residence in Chāngshā. On the night of the eighth day of the second month, he attained enlightenment.
That same night, a voice resounded from the void, announcing to the people throughout the city: "Tonight, Chan Master Huáng has attained the Way. All [heard it].
This was a disciple of the Great Master.
In the second year of the Shangyuan era, Wei Lijian, the Regional Inspector of Guangzhou, memorialized that the monk Xingtao and the transmission of the *kāṣāya* robe had entered the palace.
The Emperor, moved by filial piety, acted according to the memorial.

The Imperial Edict stated: "We decree that Caoxi Mountain’s Sixth Patriarch, who transmitted the *kāṣāya*, along with the monk Xingtao and the lay disciple Wei Li, shall be granted official transport for travel by water and land, accompanying the imperial envoy Liu Chujiang to the Capital.
Issued on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the second year of Shangyuan. Furthermore, [issued] on the first day of the first month of the second year of Qianyuan.

Master Tao submitted a memorial declining [the invitation] on account of his old age and illness. He dispatched his senior disciple Senghui and his family member Yonghe to deliver the Dharma-kāṣāya into the palace.
They followed the imperial messenger Liu Chujiang to the capital, where they were granted an audience on the eighth day of the fourth month.
Master Tao passed away on the seventeenth day of the first month; he was eighty-nine years of age. An imperial edict was issued bestowing [posthumous honors].
A pair of elephant-purple *kāṣāya* robes; the family members were granted ordination by imperial decree and assigned to this temple.
Gyeongheung-sa was renamed Gyeongneung-sa, and the hermitage of the Upādhyāya was renamed Beopok-sa by imperial decree.
Furthermore, the monk Huixiang, following the imperial envoy Liu Chujiang, delivered robes to the capital. Having completed his mission, he submitted this memorial to take leave and return home:

"The śramaṇa and subject Huixiang speaks. Your servant is a lowly individual from a remote region who has, by fortune, joined the ranks of the monastic community. I have long delighted in dwelling among the mountains and forests."
Upholding the Holy Teachings: The aforementioned robe and alms bowl have been transmitted from Master Bodhidharma down to the present day.

At all times, they were revered by the entire realm; beings throughout the *sahasra-lokadhātu* took refuge in them, and devas and humans gazed upon them with veneration. This was intended to cause later students to contemplate the person through the objects they left behind.
Although this servant is of little talent, he has unworthily received this entrustment. Only yesterday, having received the imperial decree to dispatch them to the celestial palace, [I personally...]
I shall maintain this myself forever, ensuring it never falls into ruin. My sense of gratitude and indebtedness is such that I cannot overcome my grief.
Thus we know that the robe of the Great Dharma shall not decay for ten thousand kalpas; the monastics of the capital shall wear it upon their heads and carry it forth.

However, my master Xingtao has long transmitted the seal of the Dharma and has protected this robe and bowl as if guarding a jewel in his topknot. Having repeatedly received Your Majesty’s virtuous edicts, I dare not disobey your command. One.
The Emperor has already passed away, suddenly abandoning the bright dawn of his reign.

Your servant now wishes to return there to inform the divine spirits, to proclaim the Imperial sentiments, to set forth the reasons for the presentation of robes and the reformation of the temple, and to recount our remembrance of the past and our shared compassion. In this current memorial, your servant fears that he will die ten thousand times over.
Unable to overcome my tears and longing, I have written this memorial of humble and sincere devotion to take leave of my service for Your Majesty’s information.
The śramaṇa Huixiang, deeply grieved and filled with longing, bows his head repeatedly and respectfully writes.
The Emperor, whose filial piety moves Heaven, issued an imperial decree in response to the memorial of the monk Huixiang, stating:
"The Master’s conduct as a teacher is profound and his observance of the precepts is pure and circumspect. His virtuous character is solitary and eminent;

he has transmitted the robe and alms bowl entrusted by former sages. While maintaining them in the southern regions through many changing years, he has never allowed them to be lost or neglected. I, the Emperor, am reverent..."
I truly admire the Way and have dispatched envoys to seek it from afar. You, Master, have traveled through perilous paths to deliver [the scriptures] upon your head;
how could my earnest wish bring you any comfort? Furthermore, although your physical body has perished, your spirit remains as if present.

Once you have returned there, please fully recount this spiritual efficacy so that all may know how I have honored you with reverence that shall endure forever and never decay. You should now depart in peace.

Furthermore, on the twentieth day of the eleventh month of the third year of the Ganyuan era, Emperor Xiaogong dispatched the palace messenger Cheng Jingji to deliver harmonized incense for offering before the meditation niche of Great Master Neng. An oral edict was proclaimed to burn the incense within the niche.
A single arc of rainbow light shot straight upward to a height of several zhang. When Officer Cheng saw the light, he danced with the villagers and recorded the event in a memorial for submission.
Furthermore, Emperor Baoying sent back the *kashāya* transmitted by the Dharma to Caoxi. The imperial decree stated:
(The *kashāya* had been kept at Zongchi Temple in the capital for seven years.)

Imperial Edict to Yang Jian, Senior Official: You have long resided in the southern regions; we trust you are in good health. We were moved by a dream in which we sent Chan Master Neng the Dharma-transmitting kāṣāya back to Caoxi.
We have subsequently dispatched the Palace Attendant, General of the State’s Pacification Yang Chongjing, to receive it with the utmost reverence and deliver it.
This Dharma-transmitting kāṣāya is a treasure of the state; you may enshrine it according to the Dharma at Master Neng’s own monastery.

It is hereby deposited and entrusted exclusively to those among the monastic community who have personally inherited the fundamental tenets to guard and preserve it, lest it fall into ruin or be lost.
I shall personally inquire after its well-being. Issued on the seventh day of the fifth month in the first year of the Yongtai era.
Regarding the six kinds of miraculous omens that occurred during the lifetime of the Great Master Huineng and after his passing:
as for those during his lifetime, there was a tile-kiln worker by the temple who was washing chickens at a water source; the water became defiled by contact with them.
For ten days the water did not flow. The Great Master gave instructions to the tile-makers, ordering them to burn incense and offer a vegetarian feast at the site of the spring.
As soon as his prostrations and petition were finished, the water immediately began to flow. Furthermore, the temple was passed by military troops on two occasions;

the water was defiled by their contact and remained parched for several days. After the troops had retreated and dispersed, he burned incense and offered thanks, whereupon the water flowed in gentle streams for use. Moreover—
The Master resided at Guoning Temple and Xinzhou Guoen Temple. To this day, neither of these two temples has had any sparrows, crows, or vultures.
Furthermore, on the third day of the eighth month each year, the anniversary of the Master’s passing, men and women from the villages and towns gather like clouds;
they prepare a vegetarian feast within the temple, and when the meal is concluded, everyone pays their respects and takes their leave at the stupa. In an instant, a gentle breeze suddenly—
When he arose, a rare fragrance overwhelmed the people, and clouds of smoke covered the monastery. Heaven sent down a great rain that washed away the temple and the village;
thereafter, the rain ceased to fall. Furthermore, after the Great Master’s passing, his dharma robes were stolen twice, yet before long they were returned;
the thieves could not keep them. Moreover, after the Great Master’s passing, his spiritual essence was constantly present.
It remains there; it appears as if seen in a state of trance. Within the niche and stupa, a wondrous fragrance is constantly present, and at times it enters one's dreams.
The auspicious omens preceding and following these events are too numerous to count; as many years have passed, they cannot all be fully recorded.
Afterword to the Separate Biography of the Great Master of Caoxi:

When the Great Master of Caoxi was first gathering firewood to provide for his parents, he once carried a load of wood to the market. There, he heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reaching the passage:
"One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere. He was profoundly moved and immediately set out for Huangmei. This is as recorded in various biographies.

This is all the same. However, the *Record of the Platform Sūtra* states: "At the third roll of the drum, he entered the room. The Patriarch surrounded him with his *kāṣāya* so that no one could see them, and preached the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for him.
When they reached the passage, 'One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere,' [Huineng] attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words.
Now, if he had not previously heard the sūtra and attained awakening in the marketplace, how could he have gone to Huangmei to meet the Fifth Patriarch and respond to his inquiries?
"How like a flowing stream! How much more so when one speaks of restoring [the truth] oneself? The rice has long been cooked; it merely lacks the sifting.

If one claims that the transmission of the robe was heard on the night of the sutra-recitation and only then attained awakening, then the beginning and end would not correspond, and the sequence of the text and principle would be inverted—this is deeply suspicious.

I once read the *Continued Public Discourse on the Forest Monasteries* (composed by Zhuxian Fanshan of Zhulin): "When the Sixth Patriarch was first at a market inn, he heard a guest reciting the *Golden..."*

In the *Diamond Sūtra*, upon reaching the passage "one should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he attained a sudden and expansive awakening. He subsequently sought out and visited Huangmei;
this account is recorded in the ancient version of the *Platform Sūtra* (*Tánjīng*), and its provenance remains perfectly intact.
I personally encountered it when I was seventeen or eighteen years old, but now it is entirely non-existent. Furthermore, from the time he first met Huangmei until he met Zen Master Huixiu...
The verses and other words [contained herein] are all the result of wondrous awakening to the fundamental nature and profound penetration of the source of dharmas;

they emerge uniquely from the natural state, beyond the capacity of ordinary people who have not yet awakened to express them. Now, the *Platform Sūtra* states that the Fifth Patriarch, having surrounded himself with his monastic robe so as not to let others see him, preached the *Diamond Sūtra* to him until he reached the passage:
"One should abide nowhere while giving rise to the mind. At these words, he attained immediate awakening.
I, Meng, consider these to be the words of a vulgar and base individual from the lineage of the Sixth Patriarch, who fabricated and interpolated this text by adding the two characters "jiāzhì" (恰至).
Examining his base intent, he meant that one personally awakens through the words of their teacher and personally attains the Dharma, thereby succeeding to the position of the Sixth Patriarch.
Little did he know that one possesses the wisdom of no-teacher, spontaneous wisdom, and self-attained wisdom.
"One must awaken on one's own before being fit to receive the transmission. Furthermore, it is said that he surrounded himself with his *kāṣāya* so as not to be seen by others;
was it that the *kāṣāya* possessed supernatural powers such that people could not see him?

Or is it merely a matter of following the words of the World-Honored One at the Many Sons Stūpa (*Bahuputra-caitya*), who commanded Kāśyapa to surround him with the *saṃghāṭī*? National Teacher Zhong said: "Grasp..."
The *Platform Sūtra* has been altered; it has been interpolated with vulgar talk and the sacred intent has been excised, thereby deluding later followers.

This treatise concludes [that critique]. Previously, at Tōbu, I obtained the *Separate Biography of the Great Master of Caoxi*. In ancient times, the Great Master of Dharma Transmission brought back a manuscript copied by hand from the Tang dynasty and enshrined it within the precincts of Mt.
Enryaku. Alas, on what day did it fall into neglect? It remained hidden in a sub-temple for many years until I was still young. Now, having enjoyed [the opportunity to study it]...
In the spring of the year *Hōei* (847), the Confucian scholar Yamada Daikai of Tōbu invited his fellow student Amanokawa Jōemon to tour the famous districts of the capital.
There, they happened upon this precious manuscript and transcribed it. It was then preserved with ten layers of wrapping within his family collection.
At the end of the transmission, there are the words: "Completed on the nineteenth day of the second month of the nineteenth year of *Enchū* (803); sealed by Saichō of Tiantai. Furthermore—

Three seals were affixed, engraved with the four characters "Hiei-ji. This was the nineteenth year of the Zhengyuan era, corresponding to the twentieth year of the Japanese Enryaku era, the year of the Earth-Ox (Biyou).
It had been ninety-one years from the passing of the Great Master in the second year of the Xuantian era of the Tang dynasty until the nineteenth year of Zhengyuan.
It is said that the ancient manuscript of the *Platform Sutra* had long since been lost and had circulated throughout the world [in other forms].
The *Fubao* was compiled after the Song dynasty; furthermore, the various other biographies were not composed during the Master’s own time.
Only this biography was written not long after the Great Master passed away and may thus be called a veritable record. Yet, it differs from the other biographies and the *Platform Sūtra*.

Nevertheless, when one examines the matter of the transmission of the Dharma at Huangmei—the exchange between teacher and disciple and the nature of their karmic conditions—it is truly worthy of reverence and trust. Thus, previously...
Doubts were finally dispelled. The evaluations of the immortal Zhu [Daoshi] also proved accurate; it is a pity that the name of the compiler has been lost.
Upon examining the *Catalogue of Imported Official Records*, I found that the work titled *The Biography of the Great Master of Caoxi*, in one fascicle, was indeed it.

Alas! How fortunate to have been granted access to such profound virtue! This ancient relic of a millennium has now reached our land; it is a treasure of this nation. I therefore wish to ensure its immortality.
Bestowed upon Qi Jue by [the author].
Recorded respectfully by Zu Fang in the fourth month of summer, the twelfth year of the Baoli era (1822), the year of Renwu.
